textbookText: PHYSIOLOGY OF DIGESTION The process of conversion of complex food particles into simpler absorbable or diffusible forms is digestion. This process is carried out by the organs and glands in the digestive tract. It involves both mechanical and chemical processes. Mechanical process is simply the conversion of larger food particles into smaller forms so that enzymes thoroughly act on it. Whereas the chemical process is the chemical conversion of complex organic compounds such as different types of carbohydrates, protein, fat into glucose, galactose, amino acid, fatty acid and glycerol etc. as end products. Physiology of digestion can be discussed under following heads: 1. Food: Earthworm is omnivorous and detrivorous. It feeds on soil rich in decaying organic matter such as decayed leaves, nematodes, protozoan, insect’s egg, larva and other micro-organisms. It can directly feed on leaves, grasses, algae etc. 2. Feeding:

At the time of feeding, buccal cavity is protruded or everted out and the soil with food is drawn into the mouth by sucking and pumping action of the pharynx. It is aided by the muscles around the pharynx. 3. Digestion: Ingested foods into the buccal cavity do not undergo digestion. Now, the food is passed into the pharynx which receives secretion of salivary glands. Salivary secretion contains mucus and proteolytic enzymes which lubricate food as well as digest proteins into proteoses and peptones. Now, food passes into gizzard through oesophagus by peristalsis. Gizzard acts as grinder because of its contractile muscular wall and cuticle lined lumen. It grinds or pulverizes the larger food masses into the fine powdered form. Food now reaches int o the stomach where further digestion of protein by proteolytic enzymes occurs. Semi digested food , now passes into the intestine and gets digested completely. Such food is subjected to the action of various enzymes secreted by intestine and intestinal caeca. i. Amylase: This enzyme acts upon the carbohydrates to convert them into simple sugar like glucose, fructose etc. ii. Protease: It hydrolyses proteins or proteoses and peptones into amino acid. iii. Lipase: It digests fats and converts into fatty acid and glycerol. iv. Chitinase: It digests chitin found in exoskeleton of arthropods. v. Cellulase: This enzyme digests cellulose. 4. Absorption and egestion Nutrients from digested food are absorbed by the intestinal villi, particularly by the typhlosole. After absorption, they are passed into blood capillaries in the intestinal wall and transported to the various parts of the body. Hence, intestine is the site for both the digestion and absorption of food. Undigested food materials and soil are discharged out through the anus in the form of small rounded pellets of mud called worm casting. 8.3.5 EXCRETORY OR NEPHRIDIAL SYSTEM Let’s discuss the given questions. i. What is excretion? ii. Why do animals excrete? iii. Is earthworm ammonotelic, ureotelic or uricotelic? Why? iv. What is the excretory organ of earthworms?

In the body of living beings, various waste products are generated due to metabolic activities. Such wastes should be eliminated for maintaining healthy and stable internal environment of the body. Excretion is the process of expulsion of metabolic wastes, especially nitrogenous wastes produced inside the body. Earthworm is an urecotelic and ammonotelic animal. Excretion is performed by segmentally arranged, microscopic, long, thin and much convoluted tubular units called nephridia. Nephridia of earthworm are small; called micronephridia unlike those of leech and Nereis which are larger, called meganephridia. According to the location of nephridia in the body of earthworm, they are distinguished into 3 types: pharyngeal, integumentary and septal nephridia.
1. Pharyngeal nephridia: 4th 5th and 6th segment. 2. Integumentary nephridia: Entire body wall except first few segments.
3. Septal nephridia: Attached to both the faces of each inter-segmental septum from 15/16 segment upto the last.
